Connecting an adapter, choosing your car and Android Auto

1. Plug your ELM327 adapter into the car's OBD2 port, usually under the dashboard near the steering wheel.
2. Turn the ignition on (the engine can be off).
3. Tap Connect and choose how your adapter connects.

No adapter? Tap Demo to try the app with a simulated car.

Bluetooth: tap Connect, then Bluetooth. The app lists your adapter by name, whatever kind of Bluetooth it uses. If it needs pairing, Android asks for a PIN: it\'s usually 1234 or 0000.\n\nWi-Fi: join the adapter\'s Wi-Fi network in your phone\'s settings first, then connect. The usual address is 192.168.0.10, port 35000.

Check the ignition is on and the adapter\'s light is lit. Then, on the Diagnostics tab, tap Your car and choose your car\'s make, year and model, so the app tries its usual protocol first. Cars sold in Australia before 2006 may not fully support OBD2, and some cheap adapters can\'t talk to older Fords, GM and Chrysler cars.

Android Auto only shows apps from the Play Store until you allow others. To turn that on:
1. Open Android Auto's settings on your phone (search "Android Auto" in Settings).
2. Scroll to the bottom and tap Version about 10 times, then confirm to turn on developer mode.
3. Tap the three-dot menu at the top right, then Developer settings, and turn on Unknown sources.
4. Reconnect to your car. OBD2 Reader appears in Android Auto's app list.

Connect to your adapter from the phone first, or tap Connect on the car screen to reconnect to the last one.

OBD2 Reader reads the trouble codes the engine computer, and on many cars the automatic transmission, report through the OBD2 port. It doesn\'t read other systems such as ABS, airbags or body electrics; those need the maker\'s tool or a scanner made for your make.\n\nNearly all generic codes (P0, P2, P34, U0 and U3) are explained, with causes and what to check. The few that aren\'t are named by the system they belong to. Manufacturer-specific codes (such as P1 codes) are marked as such, with where to look them up for your make, because their meaning differs between brands. A few Ford and Lincoln codes use Ford\'s own definitions, for the model years Ford\'s documents cover.

Beside the battery voltage, the app shows whether the battery looks like it's charging. Standard OBD2 has no battery-current (amps) reading, so this is an estimate from the voltage and engine speed, marked (est.).

Engine running: 13.2 V or more is charging; 12.8 to 13.2 V is charging weakly (normal on cars with smart charging, which lower the voltage while cruising); under 12.8 V is not charging; over 15.2 V is overcharging. Engine off: under 12.2 V means the battery is low.

Scan what your car reports, on this tab, shows whether your car offers any battery readings of its own.

Your location is never sent to the developer or anyone else. It\'s only saved when you record a drive and choose Save route, and then only on your phone, in that drive\'s CSV file. The app only uses it to draw the outline of your route on the drive\'s share card, and the card shows just that outline: no map, street names or coordinates. Delete the drive and its route goes with it.

OBD2 Reader only reads from your car. It never clears trouble codes, turns off the check-engine light or changes any setting, and it blocks any command that could. After a repair, a workshop scan tool can clear the codes.

Recording is off. Nothing about your drives is saved unless you tap Record drive; then every reading goes into a CSV file on this phone that you can open in Excel or Google Sheets. If you choose, the route is saved in that file too, and nowhere else. Recordings aren\'t included in phone backups.

The app can save where you drove with this recording, so you can map it in other software and see its outline on your drive card. Your location goes only into this drive\'s file on your phone, and only while it records. It\'s never sent to the developer or anyone else, and the app only uses it to draw your route\'s outline on the share card. You can delete the drive any time.
